newsitem.title: USA: New heart repair techniques gain converts.
newsitem.headline: New heart repair techniques gain converts.

text.p: New surgical techniques that avoid cracking open the chest to gain access to the heart for bypass and valve repairs are gaining converts among surgeons, as well as with patients and medical device companies.
Specialists at the American Heart Association's annual scientific sessions here cited what they described as an upsurge in interest in the procedures, known as minimally invasive heart surgery.

"There's a whole trend so that in five years we will see ...a large percentage of operations done in a minimally invasive way (due to) a combination of surgical ingenuity, patient demand...and device company ingenuity," said Lawrence Cohn, chief of the Brigham & Women's Hospital division of cardiac surgery.
Among companies racing to provide the tools needed for minimally invasive surgery in operating rooms are Heartport Inc, CardioThoracic Systems Inc, Medtronic and U.S. Surgical Corp.
"The whole field of bypass is changing and it will change forever," said Piper Jaffray medical device industry analyst Arch Smith.

While the experts here debated over the merits of new techniques that involve stopping the heart during surgery and others that work on a beating heart, they agreed that the minimially invasive approaches were winning over early skeptics.

Previously, the techniques drew only zealots and extreme skeptics, "but now there's a middle ground," said Renee Hartz of the Illinois Masonic Medical Center and author of the heart association's statement on minimally invasive heart surgery. She gave a news briefing on Tuesday.

Proponents of the beating-heart techniques, on which CardioThoracic, Medtronic and U.S. Surgical are working, cited the benefits of eliminating the need for a heart-lung machine, thus avoiding the complications that that hook-up can bring.

James Magovern, associate professor of surgery at Allegheny University of the Health Sciences, presented results at the meeting of a study comparing traditional bypass operations -- involving opening the breastbone, stopping the heart and hooking the patient up to a heart-lung machine -- with so-called beating-heart "keyhole" surgery.
The keyhole technique allows surgeons to operate on a beating heart via a window through the ribcage created by an incision about three inches (seven centimeters) long.

Magovern said patients in the study receiving the keyhole surgery had fewer complications, such as respiratory problems, spent less time in the hospital, and accounted for about 40 percent lower hospital costs, compared with those receiving the traditional bypass.

But proponents of minimally invasive techniques that stop the heart, on which Heartport is working, argue that it will be difficult to do more than a single bypass, or other repairs such as valve replacements, on a beating heart.

"We feel the need to continue using the heart-lung machine," said Bruce Reitz, chair of cardiothoracic surgery at Stanford University. It "allows (surgeons) to extend the bypass to more than one vessel, open the heart and operate on the valves."
Reitz heads a team at Stanford working with Heartport technology.

The Stanford researchers cited among the first 10 patients in a Phase I trial a patient who successfully underwent a multiple bypass using the minimally invasive technique. They said the 48-year-old man was possibly the first patient in the world to undergo a multiple bypass using the Heartport technique.
With the techniques still in early stages, industry analysts say it's too soon to determine which of the minimally invasive procedures will gain most use.
"It's premature to say who the winners and losers are," Smith said.
